blocks.text: Chapter 2 portrays the rise of false teachers who introduce destructive heresies while promising freedom to their followers. These teachers exploit their audiences through covetousness and feigned words, yet they themselves remain enslaved to corruption. The chapter's fundamental claim is that divine judgment against them is certain: their sentence has long been determined, and their destruction does not sleep.

The author establishes divine precedent through the example of sinful angels. God did not spare them but cast them into Tartarus, consigning them to pits of darkness where they are reserved for judgment. This example demonstrates that even the most powerful created beings face inevitable divine punishment for transgression.

sections.title: Noah: Herald of Righteousness in a Drowning World

blocks.text: Noah exemplifies both the futility of righteous preaching in the face of widespread ungodliness and God's fidelity to rescue the righteous. Called a herald of righteousness, Noah preached to a world bent on lawlessness, yet his message did not prevent the flood. God preserved Noah and seven others when judgment came upon the ungodly world, showing the dual pattern: judgment for the corrupt, deliverance for the faithful.

sections.title: Sodom and Gomorrah: Example and Rescue

blocks.text: Sodom and Gomorrah exemplify the totality of divine judgment: their cities were turned to ashes in an overwhelming act of condemnation, making them a standing example for those who would live ungodly. Yet within this narrative of judgment stands Lot, the righteous man, distressed by the lawless deeds surrounding him. God delivered Lot from destruction, his righteous soul vexed daily by the corrupt behavior of the wicked around him. The pattern repeats: divine judgment on the ungodly, divine rescue for the righteous.

sections.title: False Teachers Likened to Irrational Animals

blocks.text: The false teachers are portrayed as creatures without reason, animals born for capture and destruction. They rail against matters they do not understand, and their degradation is complete: they are compared to a dog returning to its vomit and a sow washed only to return to wallowing in mud. These images capture their fundamental irrationality and their inevitable downward trajectory.

sections.title: Profit-Seeking and the Way of Balaam

blocks.text: The false teachers follow the way of Balaam, son of Beor, who illustrates the condemnation of profit-seeking wrongdoing. The account includes even a speaking donkey, underscoring the absurdity and shame of pursuing gain through false prophecy. This example indicts those who would compromise their calling for financial advantage.

A particular tragedy emerges when those who have escaped the defilements of the world through knowledge of Christ become re-entangled in those same corruptions. Such re-entanglement results in a final state worse than their initial condition, suggesting a trajectory of spiritual degradation for those who reject their deliverance.
